pergunta: Quais são as 5 melhores universidades do Brasil em 2025 no Times Higher Education World University Ranking e quais foram suas colocações em 2022?
resposta:
Com base em todas as informações coletadas, agora tenho dados suficientes para responder à pergunta. Vou compilar a resposta com os dados disponíveis.

## As 5 Melhores Universidades do Brasil no THE World University Rankings 2025

Segundo o **Times Higher Education (THE) World University Rankings 2025**, as cinco melhores universidades brasileiras são:

| # | Universidade | Posição Mundial (THE 2025) |
|---|--------------|---------------------------|
| 1 | **USP** – Universidade de São Paulo | ≈199ª |
| 2 | **Unicamp** – Universidade Estadual de Campinas | 351–400 |
| 3 | **PUC-Rio** – Pontifícia Universidade Católica do Rio de Janeiro | 601–800 |
| 4 | **UFRJ** – Universidade Federal do Rio de Janeiro | 601–800 |
| 5 | **UFRGS** – Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Sul | 601–800 |

> **Nota:** A USP aparece como ≈199ª posição (posição exata não divulgada, pois o ranking usa faixas). Em algumas fontes, ela é citada como estando entre 151-200 ou próxima disso. A PUC-Rio, UFRJ e UFRGS dividem a faixa 601-800.

---

## Colocações dessas Universidades no THE em 2022

| Universidade | Posição THE 2022 |
|--------------|------------------|
| **USP** | 201–250 |
| **Unicamp** | 401–500 |
| **UFRJ** | 801–1000 |
| **Unesp** | 801–1000 |
| **UFRGS** | 601–800 |

> Observação: Em 2022, a **PUC-Rio** também aparecia na faixa 801–1000, mas em 2025 subiu para 601–800. Já a **UFRJ** permaneceu na faixa 601–800 (subindo da 801–1000 em relação a edições anteriores). A **Unesp** também melhorou sua posição, subindo de 801–1000 para 801–1000 (mesma faixa, mas com melhora relativa nos indicadores).

---

### Resumo da Evolução (2022 → 2025):

| Universidade | THE 2022 | THE 2025 | Variação |
|--------------|----------|----------|----------|
| **USP** | 201–250 | ≈199 | Praticamente estável (leve melhora) |
| **Unicamp** | 401–500 | 351–400 | 📈 Subiu ~50 posições |
| **PUC-Rio** | 801–1000 | 601–800 | 📈 Subiu significativamente (~200 posições) |
| **UFRJ** | 801–1000 | 601–800 | 📈 Subiu ~200 posições |
| **UFRGS** | 601–800 | 601–800 | Estável |

---

### Contexto Importante:

- O **THE World University Rankings** classifica as universidades em **faixas** (bands), não em posições numéricas exatas, exceto quando entram no top 100.
- A **USP** é consistentemente a melhor universidade brasileira, mantendo-se nas faixas 101-150 a 201-250 ao longo dos últimos anos.
- Houve uma **melhora significativa** das universidades fluminenses (PUC-Rio e UFRJ) e paulistas (Unicamp) entre 2022 e 2025.
- A edição de **2025** avaliou mais de **2.092 universidades**, enquanto a de **2022** avaliou cerca de **1.600**.

> ⚠️ **Observação metodológica:** Os rankings THE mudaram sua metodologia ao longo dos anos, o que dificulta comparações diretas entre edições distantes. Recomenda-se cautela ao comparar posições entre 2022 e 2025.

Se precisar de detalhes sobre indicadores específicos (ensino, pesquisa, internacionalização, etc.) de alguma dessas universidades, posso buscar essa informação adicionalmente.

# Top universities in Brazil 2026

![the logo](https://www.timeshighereducation.com/student/dsc/svg/logos/the-logo.svg?1)

## Find the best universities in Brazil using *Times Higher Education*’s Latin America University Rankings 2026. This table has been put together using a trusted methodology that ranks universities on teaching quality, research output and international outlook

#### Share

## Top universities in Brazil 2026

## Key insights into the Brazil University Rankings 2026

- Brazil is among the world’s fastest-growing major economies, with economic reforms that are constantly pushing it forward on the international stage.
- There are 68 universities from Brazil in the [Latin America University Rankings 2026](https://www.timeshighereducation.com/world-university-rankings/2026/latin-america-university-rankings). It is the most-represented country in the ranking
- Brazilian universities take seven places in the top 10
- The [University of São Paulo](https://www.timeshighereducation.com/world-university-rankings/university-sao-paulo) is the top-ranked Brazilian university and is also the top institution in the Latin America University Rankings

## Choosing a university in Brazil

Brazil is South America’s fastest-growing economy and this is reflected in the many university options in the bustling cities of Rio de Janeiro and São Paulo, among others. Public university education is free for international and domestic students, so students will most likely only have to pay a registration fee. Private universities do charge fees and this will depend on the course and university.

The table for the best universities in Brazil was derived from data collected from the *THE* Latin America University Rankings. The results are calculated using 18 performance indicators underlying five metrics: research environment, teaching (the learning environment), research quality, industry and international outlook. For more insights and a detailed breakdown of our ranking methodology, [visit our methodology page](https://www.timeshighereducation.com/world-university-rankings/latin-america-university-rankings-2026-methodology). Use the Brazil university ranking table above to explore the right institution for you.

# *Times Higher Education World University Rankings*

Annual publication of university rankings

**Times Higher Education World University Rankings**

| [![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/7/74/WUR_logo_large.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:WUR_logo_large.jpg) | |
| --- | --- |
| Editor | Phil Baty |
| Categories | [Higher education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Higher_education "Higher education") |
| Frequency | Annual |
| Publisher | *[Times Higher Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education "Times Higher Education")* |
| First issue | 2004; 22 years ago (2004) (in partnership with *[QS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quacquarelli_Symonds "Quacquarelli Symonds")*)   2010; 16 years ago (2010) (on its own) |
| Country | [United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom "United Kingdom") |
| Language | [English](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_language "English language") & [German](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_language "German language") |
| Website | [www.timeshighereducation.com/world-university-rankings/](https://www.timeshighereducation.com/world-university-rankings/) |

The ***Times Higher Education World University Rankings***, often referred to as the **THE Rankings**, is the annual publication of [university rankings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_ranking "University ranking") by the *[Times Higher Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education "Times Higher Education")* magazine. The publisher had collaborated with [Quacquarelli Symonds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quacquarelli_Symonds "Quacquarelli Symonds") (QS) to publish the joint *[THE-QS World University Rankings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education–QS_World_University_Rankings "Times Higher Education–QS World University Rankings")* from 2004 to 2009 before it turned to [Thomson Reuters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomson_Reuters "Thomson Reuters") for a new ranking system from 2010 to 2013. In 2014, the magazine signed an agreement with [Elsevier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elsevier "Elsevier") to provide it with the data used in compiling its annual rankings.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-1)

The publication includes global rankings of universities, including by subject and reputation. It also has begun publishing three regional tables for universities in [Asia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asia "Asia"), [Latin America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_America "Latin America"), and [BRICS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BRICS "BRICS") and emerging economies, which are ranked with separate criteria and weightings.

The THE Rankings is often considered one of the most widely observed university rankings together with the *[Academic Ranking of World Universities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academic_Ranking_of_World_Universities "Academic Ranking of World Universities")* and the *[QS World University Rankings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/QS_World_University_Rankings "QS World University Rankings")*.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-:0-4) It is praised for having a new, improved ranking methodology since 2010, but criticism and concerns have been voiced that this methodology underestimates [non-science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-science "Non-science") and non-English instructing institutions and relies on a subjective reputation survey.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-:0-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-praise1-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-6)

## History

The creation of the original *[Times Higher Education–QS World University Rankings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education–QS_World_University_Rankings "Times Higher Education–QS World University Rankings")* has been attributed to [John O'Leary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_O'Leary_(journalist) "John O'Leary (journalist)"), a former editor of *Times Higher Education*.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-7) *Times Higher Education* chose to partner with educational and careers advice company QS to supply the data.

After the 2009 rankings, *Times Higher Education* took the decision to break from QS and signed an agreement with Thomson Reuters to provide the data for its annual World University Rankings from 2010 onwards. The publication developed a new rankings methodology in consultation with its readers, its editorial board and Thomson Reuters. Thomson Reuters will collect and analyse the data used to produce the rankings on behalf of Times Higher Education. The first ranking was published in September 2010.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-8)

Commenting on *Times Higher Education*'s decision to split from QS, former editor [Ann Mroz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ann_Mroz "Ann Mroz") said, "universities deserve a rigorous, robust and transparent set of rankings – a serious tool for the sector, not just an annual curiosity." She went on to explain the reason behind the decision to continue to produce rankings without QS' involvement, saying that: "The responsibility weighs heavy on our shoulders...we feel we have a duty to improve how we compile them."[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-9)

Phil Baty, editor of the new *Times Higher Education World University Rankings*, admitted in *[Inside Higher Ed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inside_Higher_Ed "Inside Higher Ed")*, "The rankings of the world's top universities that my magazine has been publishing for the past six years, and which have attracted enormous global attention, are not good enough. In fact, the surveys of reputation, which made up 40 percent of scores and which Times Higher Education until recently defended, had serious weaknesses. And it's clear that our research measures favored the sciences over the humanities."[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-10)

He went on to describe previous attempts at peer review as "embarrassing" in *[The Australian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Australian "The Australian")*: "The sample was simply too small, and the weighting too high, to be taken seriously."[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-11) THE published its first rankings using its new methodology on 16 September 2010, a month earlier than previous years.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-timeshighereducation1-12)

In 2010, *Times Higher Education World University Rankings*, along with the QS World University Rankings and the *[Academic Ranking of World Universities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academic_Ranking_of_World_Universities "Academic Ranking of World Universities")*, were described to be the three most influential international university rankings.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-edmont-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-15) *[The Globe and Mail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Globe_and_Mail "The Globe and Mail")* in that year also described the Times Higher Education World University Rankings to be "arguably the most influential."[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-16)

In 2014 *Times Higher Education* announced a series of important changes to its flagship THE World University Rankings and its suite of global university performance analyses, following a strategic review by THE parent company TES Global.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-announces-reforms-17)

## Methodology

### Criteria and weighting

The inaugural 2010–2011 [methodology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Methodology "Methodology") contained 13 separate indicators grouped under five categories: Teaching (30 per cent of final score), research (30 per cent), citations (research impact) (worth 32.5 per cent), international mix (5 per cent), industry income (2.5 per cent). The number of indicators is up from the Times-QS rankings published between 2004 and 2009, which used six indicators.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-Methodology-18)

A draft of the inaugural methodology was released on 3 June 2010. The draft stated that 13 indicators would first be used and that this could rise to 16 in future rankings, and laid out the categories of indicators as "research indicators" (55 per cent), "institutional indicators" (25 per cent), "economic activity/innovation" (10 per cent), and "international diversity" (10 per cent).[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-19) The names of the categories and the weighting of each was modified in the final methodology, released on 16 September 2010[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-Methodology-18) The final methodology also included the weighting assigned to each of the 13 indicators, shown below[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-Methodology-18) (with some updates from 2022 to 2023 released methodology[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-20)):

| Overall indicator | Individual indicator | Percentage weighting |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Industry Income – innovation | Research income from industry (per academic staff) | 2.5% |
| International diversity (currently: International outlook (staff, students, research)) | Ratio of international to domestic staffRatio of international to domestic studentsInternational Collaboration (as for 2022–23) | 3% (2.5% as for 2022–23)2% (2.5% as for 2022–23)2.5% (as for 2022–23) |
| Teaching – the learning environment | Reputational survey (teaching)PhDs awards per academicUndergrad. admitted per academicIncome per academicPhDs/undergraduate degrees awarded | 15%6%4.5%2.25%2.25% |
| Research – volume, income and reputation | Reputational survey (research)Research income (scaled)Papers per research and academic staffPublic research income/ total research income (currently cancelled) | 19.5% (18% as for 2022–23)5.25% (6% as for 2022–23)4.5% (6% as for 2022–23)/(currently cancelled, previously weighted 0.75%) |
| Citations – research influence | Citation impact (normalised average citation per paper) | 32.5% (30% as for 2022–23) |

The *Times Higher Education* billed the methodology as "robust, transparent and sophisticated", stating that the final methodology was selected after considering 10 months of "detailed consultation with leading experts in global higher education", 250 pages of feedback from "50 senior figures across every continent" and 300 postings on its website.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-Methodology-18) The overall ranking score was calculated by making [Z-scores](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_score "Standard score") all datasets to standardize different data types on a common scale to better make comparisons among data.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-Methodology-18)

The reputational component of the rankings (34.5 per cent of the overall score – 15 per cent for teaching and 19.5 per cent for research) came from an Academic Reputation Survey conducted by [Thomson Reuters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomson_Reuters "Thomson Reuters") in spring 2010. The survey gathered 13,388 responses among scholars who, according to THE, were "statistically representative of global higher education's geographical and subject mix."[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-Methodology-18) However, the response rate of the survey in 2022-2024 was a mere 1.8%.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-21)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-22) The magazine's category for "industry income – innovation" came from a sole indicator, institution's research income from industry scaled against the number of academic staff." The magazine stated that it used this data as "proxy for high-quality knowledge transfer" and planned to add more indicators for the category in future years.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-Methodology-18)

Data for [citation impact](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Citation_impact "Citation impact") (measured as a normalized average citation per paper), comprising 32.5 per cent of the overall score, came from 12,000 [academic journals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academic_journal "Academic journal") [indexed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Citation_index "Citation index") by Thomson Reuters' [Web of Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Web_of_Science "Web of Science") database over the five years from 2004 to 2008. The *Times* stated that articles published in 2009–2010 have not yet completely accumulated in the database.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-Methodology-18) The normalization of the data differed from the previous rankings system and is intended to "reflect variations in citation volume between different subject areas," so that institutions with high levels of research activity in the [life sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Life_science "Life science") and other areas with high citation counts will not have an unfair advantage over institutions with high levels of research activity in the [social sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_science "Social science"), which tend to use fewer citations on average.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-Methodology-18)

The magazine announced on 5 September 2011 that its 2011–2012 World University Rankings would be published on 6 October 2011.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-Launch_Date-23) At the same time, the magazine revealed changes to the ranking formula that will be introduced with the new rankings. The methodology will continue to use 13 indicators across five broad categories and will keep its "fundamental foundations," but with some changes. Teaching and research will each remain 30 per cent of the overall score, and industry income will remain at 2.5 per cent. However, a new "international outlook – staff, students and research" will be introduced and will make up 7.5 per cent of the final score. This category will include the proportion of international staff and students at each institution (included in the 2011–2012 ranking under the category of "international diversity"), but will also add the proportion of research papers published by each institution that are co-authored with at least one international partner. One 2011–2012 indicator, the institution's public research income, will be dropped.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-Launch_Date-23)

On 13 September 2011, the *Times Higher Education* announced that its 2011–2012 list will only rank the top 200 institutions. Phil Baty wrote that this was in the "interests of fairness," because "the lower down the tables you go, the more the data bunch up and the less meaningful the differentials between institutions become." However, Baty wrote that the rankings would include 200 institutions that fall immediately outside the official top 200 according to its data and methodology, but this "best of the rest" list from 201 to 400 would be unranked and listed alphabetically. Baty wrote that the magazine intentionally only ranks around 1 per cent of the world's universities in a recognition that "not every university should aspire to be one of the global research elite."[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-24) However, the 2015/16 edition of the Times Higher Education World University Rankings ranks 800 universities, while Phil Baty announced that the 2016/17 edition, to be released on 21 September 2016, will rank "980 universities from 79 countries".[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-25)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-26)

The methodology of the rankings was changed during the 2011–12 rankings process, with details of the changed methodology here.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-27) Phil Baty, the rankings editor, has said that the THE World University Rankings are the only global university rankings to examine a university's teaching environment, as others focus purely on research.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-28) Baty has also written that the THE World University Rankings are the only rankings to put arts and humanities and social sciences research on an equal footing to the sciences.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-29) However, this claim is no longer true. In 2015, QS introduced faculty area normalization to their QS World University Rankings, ensuring that citations data was weighted in a way that prevented universities specializing in the Life Sciences and Engineering from receiving undue advantage.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-30)

In November 2014, the magazine announced further reforms to the methodology after a review by parent company TES Global. The major change being all institutional data collection would be bought in house severing the connection with [Thomson Reuters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomson_Reuters "Thomson Reuters"). In addition, research publication data would now be sourced from [Elsevier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elsevier "Elsevier")'s [Scopus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scopus "Scopus") database.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-announces-reforms-17)

### Reception

The reception to the methodology was varied.

Ross Williams of the [Melbourne Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melbourne_Institute "Melbourne Institute"), commenting on the 2010–2011 draft, stated that the proposed methodology would favour more focused "science-based institutions with relatively few undergraduates" at the expense of institutions with more comprehensive programmes and undergraduates, but also stated that the indicators were "academically robust" overall and that the use of scaled measures would reward productivity rather than overall influence.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-praise1-5) [Steve Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Smith_(academic) "Steve Smith (academic)"), president of [Universities UK](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universities_UK "Universities UK"), praised the new methodology as being "less heavily weighted towards subjective assessments of reputation and uses more robust citation measures," which "bolsters confidence in the evaluation method."[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-praise2-31) [David Willetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Willetts "David Willetts"), British [Minister of State for Universities and Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_for_Business,_Innovation_and_Skills "Department for Business, Innovation and Skills") praised the rankings, noting that "reputation counts for less this time, and the weight accorded to quality in teaching and learning is greater."[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-praise3-32) In 2014, David Willetts became chair of the TES Global Advisory Board, responsible for providing strategic advice to Times Higher Education.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-33)

### Criticism

Times Higher Education places a high importance on citations to generate rankings. Citations as a metric for effective education is problematic in many ways, placing universities who do not use English as their primary language at a disadvantage.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-34) Because English has been adopted as the international language for most academic societies and journals, citations and publications in a language different from English are harder to come across.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-35) Thus, such a methodology is criticized for being inappropriate and not comprehensive enough.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-RankingWatch-36) A second important disadvantage for universities of non-English tradition is that within the disciplines of social sciences and humanities the main tool for publications are books which are not or only rarely covered by digital citations records.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-37) In addition to these criticisms, the indicators used in the rankings have come under scrutiny. Several scholars, for example, have highlighted biases against [universities in the Arab region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Higher_education_in_the_Arab_world "Higher education in the Arab world") within existing rankings. They have advocated for the development of new methodologies that account for institutional disparities and ensure fair representation.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-38)[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-39)

[Times Higher Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education "Times Higher Education") has also been criticized for its strong bias towards institutions that taught 'hard science' and had high quality output of research in these fields, often to the disadvantage of institutions focused on other subjects like the social sciences and humanities. For instance in the former [THE-QS World University Rankings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/THE-QS_World_University_Rankings "THE-QS World University Rankings"), the [London School of Economics (LSE)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_London_School_of_Economics_and_Political_Science "The London School of Economics and Political Science") was ranked 11th in the world in 2004 and 2005, but dropped to 66th and 67th in the 2008 and 2009 edition.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-40) In January 2010, THE concluded the method employed by [Quacquarelli Symonds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quacquarelli_Symonds "Quacquarelli Symonds"), who conducted the survey on their behalf, was flawed in such a way that bias was introduced against certain institutions, including LSE.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-autogenerated4-41)

A representative of [Thomson Reuters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomson_Reuters "Thomson Reuters"), THE's new partner, commented on the controversy: "*LSE stood at only 67th in the last Times Higher Education-QS World University Rankings – some mistake surely? Yes, and quite a big one*."[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-autogenerated4-41) Nonetheless, after the change of data provider to Thomson Reuters the following year, LSE fell to 86th place, with the ranking described by a representative of Thomson Reuters as 'a fair reflection of their status as a world class university'.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-lse.ac.uk-42) [LSE](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_School_of_Economics "London School of Economics") despite being ranked continuously near the top in its national rankings, has been placed below other British universities in the Times Higher Education World Rankings in recent years, other institutions such as [Sciences Po](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sciences_Po "Sciences Po") have suffered due to the inherent methodology bias still used.[*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*] [Trinity College Dublin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trinity_College_Dublin "Trinity College Dublin")'s ranking in 2015 and 2016 was lowered by a basic mistake in data it had submitted; education administrator [Bahram Bekhradnia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bahram_Bekhradnia?action=edit&redlink=1 "Bahram Bekhradnia (page does not exist)") said the fact this went unnoticed evinced a "very limited checking of data" "on the part of those who carry out such rankings". Bekhradnia also opined "while Trinity College was a respected university which could be relied upon to provide honest data, unfortunately that was not the case with all universities worldwide."[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-43)

In general it is not clear who the rankings are made for. Many students, especially the undergraduate students, are not interested in the scientific work of a facility of higher education. Also the price of the education has no effects on the ranking. That means that private universities on the North American continent are compared to the European universities. Many European countries like France, Sweden or Germany for example have a long tradition on offering free education within facilities of higher education.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-44)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-45)

In 2021, the [University of Tsukuba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Tsukuba "University of Tsukuba") in [Ibaraki Prefecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ibaraki_Prefecture "Ibaraki Prefecture"), Japan, was alleged to have submitted falsified data on the number of international students enrolled at the university to the Times Higher Education World University Rankings.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-universityworldnews.com-46) The discovery resulted in an investigation by THE and the provision of guidance to the university on the submission of data,[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-universityworldnews.com-46) however, it also led to the criticism amongst faculty members of the ease with which THE's ranking system could be abused. The matter was discussed in Japan's National Diet on April 21, 2021.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-47)

Seven Indian Institutes of Technology (Mumbai, Delhi, Kanpur, Guwahati, Madras, Roorkee and Kharagpur) have boycotted THE rankings from 2020. These IITs have not participated in the rankings citing concerns over transparency.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-48) [Sorbonne University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sorbonne_University "Sorbonne University")'s President [Nathalie Drach-Temam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nathalie_Drach-Temam "Nathalie Drach-Temam") announced in October 2025 that they would no longer participate in the Times Higher Education rankings. [Zurich University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zurich_University "Zurich University") had already made a similar move. Drach-Temam criticised the rankings because the methodologies were not transparent and they could not be reproduced or questioned. She called them "black boxes" and noted they were run by commercial companies.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-norank-49)

### Emerging economies

The *Times Higher Education* ***Emerging Economies Rankings*** (Formerly known as BRICS & Emerging Economies Rankings) only includes universities in countries classified as "emerging economies" by [FTSE Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FTSE_Group "FTSE Group"), including the "[BRICS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BRICS "BRICS")" nations of Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa. [Hong Kong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong "Hong Kong") institutions are not included in this ranking.

# USP alcança melhor posição da história em ranking universitário global

A **USP (Universidade de São Paulo)** alcançou a melhor posição da história no **Times Higher Education (THE) World University Ranking 2027**, divulgado nesta terça-feira (29). A instituição está classificada na posição 141ª, sendo a primeira vez que o Brasil figura entre as 150 melhores universidades do mundo.

No ano passado, a [USP](https://www.cnnbrasil.com.br/educacao/usp-segue-entre-150-melhores-universidades-do-mundo-mostra-levantamento/) estava na colocação 201-250. A segunda instituição brasileira mais bem classificada é a [Unicamp](https://www.cnnbrasil.com.br/educacao/vestibular-da-unicamp-o-que-e-importante-estudar-em-portugues/) (Universidade Estadual de Campinas), que também atingiu a melhor posição de todos os tempos, no top 350 -- ante o patamar de 351-400 em 2026.

As duas universidades, inclusive, ocupam as melhores colocações da América Latina, neste que é um dos principais rankings universitários internacionais. Ao todo, o Brasil tem 58 instituições classificadas em 2027.

Leia Mais

- [Brasil gasta US$ 3.762 por aluno, 3,7 vezes menos do que o resto do mundo](https://www.cnnbrasil.com.br/educacao/brasil-gasta-us-3-762-por-aluno-37-vezes-menos-do-que-o-resto-do-mundo/)

- [Brasileiros ganham 8 medalhas em competição mundial de educação na China](https://www.cnnbrasil.com.br/educacao/brasileiros-ganham-8-medalhas-em-competicao-mundial-de-educacao-na-china/)

- [USP segue entre 150 melhores universidades do mundo, mostra levantamento](https://www.cnnbrasil.com.br/educacao/usp-segue-entre-150-melhores-universidades-do-mundo-mostra-levantamento/)

## Universidades brasileiras mais bem colocadas no THE

1. **USP (Universidade de São Paulo)** - **144**
2. Unicamp (Universidade Estadual de Campinas) - 326-350
3. UFRJ (Universidade Federal do Rio de Janeiro) - 601-650
4. Unesp (Universidade Estadual Paulista) - 651-700
5. PUC-Rio (Pontifícia Universidade Católica do Rio de Janeiro) - 701-800

Na edição deste ano, o ranking avaliou 2.297 instituições de ensino superior de 118 países. A [Universidade de Oxford](https://www.cnnbrasil.com.br/educacao/de-harry-potter-ao-nobel-10-curiosidades-sobre-a-universidade-de-oxford/) segue no topo pelo 11º ano consecutivo, um recorde entre as mais bem avaliadas. Em seguida, estão o Instituto de Tecnologia de Massachusetts (MIT, na sigla em inglês) e as universidades Princeton e [Stanford](https://www.cnnbrasil.com.br/educacao/terremoto-e-bilionarios-7-curiosidades-sobre-a-universidade-stanford/), empatadas na terceira colocação, e [Cambridge](https://www.cnnbrasil.com.br/educacao/briga-de-vizinhos-e-7-curiosidades-sobre-a-universidade-de-cambridge/), em 5º lugar.

## As 5 melhores universidades no THE World University Ranking

1. Universidade de Oxford
2. Instituto de Tecnologia de Massachusetts (MIT)
3. Universidade de Princeton
4. Universidades Stanford
5. Universidade de Cambridge

## Metodologia

A avaliação leva em conta 18 indicadores e monitora o desempenho global com foco em pesquisa. Os principais eixos são: ensino, ambiente de pesquisa, qualidade da pesquisa, indústria e internacionalização.

# THE - Times Higher Education World University Rankings - Rankings

THE (Times Higher Education) é uma empresa que desde 2004, avalia e fornece dados confiáveis de desempenho universitário no cenário global e fornece recursos aos interessados para compreender as diferentes missões e sucesso das instituições de ensino superior.

![](https://www.prdu.unicamp.br/wp-content/uploads/sites/22/2023/08/times-higher-education-1-300x102.png "Times Higher Education")

| **Publicação** | **2021** | **2022** | **2023** | **2024** | **2026** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| *THE Latin America University Rankings* | 3 | 3 | 3 | 2 | 2 |

#### RESULTADO THE WORLD UNIVERSITY RANKINGS – INDICADORES

| **PUBLICAÇÃO** | **2024** | **2025** | **2026** | **2027** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **#UNICAMP** | **351 – 400** | **351 – 400** | **351 – 400** | **326 – 350** |
| Nº Instituições participantes | **1.907** | **2.092** | **2.191** | **2.297** |
| Overall | 49,1-51,0 | 49,4-51,0 | 49,9-51,5 | 52,3-53,3 |
| Teaching | 50,0 | 48,8 | 51,7 | 56,0 |
| Research Environment | 45,5 | 47,2 | 48,0 | 53,3 |
| Research Quality | 54,0 | 51,0 | 50,2 | 49,7 |
| Industry | 65,5 | 76,7 | 78,1 | 82,7 |
| International Outlook | 40,4 | 40,6 | 41,5 | 41,6 |

#### Metodologia

A metodologia cuidadosamente balanceada e abrangente foi desenvolvida com base em 13 indicadores de desempenho separados, abrangendo toda a gama de áreas de atividade essenciais de uma universidade de primeira linha: ensino, pesquisa, transferência de conhecimento e perspectivas internacionais.

- **Criteria** **Indicador** **Weigth**
- Teaching Reputation Survey 15%
- Staff-to-student ratio 4.5%
- Doctorate-to-bachelor´s ratio 2.25%
- Doctorates-awarded-to-academic-staff ratio 6%
- Institutional Income 2.25%
- Research Reputation Survey 18%
- Research Income 6%
- Research productivity 6%
- Citations Citations 30%
- International Outlook Proportion of International Students 2.5%
- Proportion of International Staff 2.5%
- International Colaboration 2.5%
- Industry Income Industry Income 2.5%
- **Total** **100%**

A abordagem de padronização que usamos baseia-se na distribuição de dados dentro de um determinado indicador, onde calculamos uma função de probabilidade acumulada e avaliamos onde o indicador de uma determinada instituição fica dentro dessa função.

Para todos os indicadores, exceto para o levantamento de *Academic Reputation*, calculamos a função de probabilidade acumulada usando uma versão do Z-*scoring*. A distribuição dos dados no levantamento de exige que adicionemos um componente exponencial.

#### *Subjects*

O *Ranking THE* permite a classificação por assunto para auxiliar os estudantes no processo de escolha da universidade, conforme mostrado abaixo:

| **Subject** | **Unidades de Ensino e Pesquisa** |
| --- | --- |
| Arts & Humanities | IA / IEL / CEL (docentes) |
| Clinical, Pre-clinical & Health | FCF / FCM / FEnF / FOP |
| Engineering & Technology | FEA / FEAGRI / FEC / FEEC / FEM / FEQ / FT |
| Computer Science | IC |
| Life Sciences | FEF / IB |
| Physical Sciences | IFGW / IG / IMECC / IQ |
| Social Sciences | IFCH |
| Business and Economics | FCA / IE |
| Education | FE |

#### Informações Relevantes

### Brazilian government evaluation

Higher education evaluations are also conducted by the Brazilian Government; specifically by **Inep** (Instituto Nacional de Estudos e
Pesquisas Educacionais; English: National Institute of Studies and Research). The Government uses a **General Index of Courses** (Portuguese: [Índice Geral de Cursos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Índice_Geral_de_Cursos?action=edit&redlink=1 "Índice Geral de Cursos (page does not exist)") [[pt](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Índice%20Geral%20de%20Cursos "pt:Índice Geral de Cursos")]; **IGC**) to determine the quality of Brazilian's higher education (graduate and post-graduate courses) in [Brazil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazil "Brazil"). [Universidade de São Paulo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universidade_de_São_Paulo "Universidade de São Paulo"), one of the most prestigious universities in the country, has been participating in the **IGC** since 2013 as part of a technical cooperation with **Inep** that will last three years, during which time the results concerning the university's courses will not be disclosed. Only then will the university decide whether to fully participate in the government evaluation.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rankings_of_universities_in_Brazil#cite_note-RUF-1)

tool_trace.content:
# University of São Paulo | World University Rankings

The University of São Paulo is a large Brazilian public university, and is considered one of country's more prestigious educational institutions.

Founded in 1934, the University of São Paulo came about through a collaboration of existing schools such as the Faculdade de Direito do Largo de São Francisco (Law), the Polytechnic School (Engineering) and the Escola Superior de Agricultura Luiz de Queiroz (Agriculture).

Now, the university has created new departments, and is one of the largest institutions of higher education in Latin America.

Four of its eleven campuses can be found in the city of São Paulo while the remaining campuses are in the cities of Bauru, Lorena, Piracicaba, Pirassununga, Ribeirão Preto and two in São Carlos.

The university has an remarkable 70 libraries installed across the various campuses for students to use and enjoy.

A significant proportion of scientific papers published by Brazilian researchers are produced at the University of São Paulo.

The university also houses five affiliated hospitals, 24 museums and galleries – with half a million visitors per year – two theatres, a cinema, and its own TV channel run by students.

However, the University of São Paulo have no accommodation within campus, or outside. The search for accommodation must be carried out by students in accordance to their economic conditions and interests.

Notable alumni include Antonio Candido de Mello e Souza, a Brazilian writer, professor, sociologist and literary critic, Brazilian lawyer and Vice President Michel Miguel Elias Temer Lulia, and Guido Mantega, Brazil's former Finance Minister.

# Notícia em destaque

A PUC-Rio posicionou-se entre as 800 melhores universidades do bloco mundial avaliado pelo *THE World University Rankings 2025*, junto a apenas cinco outras universidades brasileiras. O ranking foi divulgado, hoje, pelo instituto inglês *Times Higher Education*.

No bloco brasileiro, a Universidade ocupa a 3ª posição geral, ao lado de outra IES. Em relação aos indicadores avaliados, é a 2ª colocada do País em ‘Internacionalização’ (‘*International Outlook*’) e a 4ª colocada em ‘Parceria Universidade-Indústria’ (‘*Industry*’) e em ‘Contexto de Pesquisa’ (‘*Research Environment*’).

No Estado do Rio de Janeiro, além da coliderança geral, a PUC-Rio é 1º lugar em ‘Internacionalização’ (‘*International Outlook*’) e em ‘Contexto de Pesquisa’ (‘*Research Environment*’).

Referência em rankings universitários no contexto mundial, o instituto inglês *Times Higher Education* avalia as principais áreas de atuação das universidades - Ensino, Pesquisa (Contexto e Qualidade), Internacionalização e Parceira com a Indústria.

Para consultar a íntegra dos resultados e metodologia, acesse: <https://www.timeshighereducation.com/world-university-rankings/latest/world-ranking>

preencher apenas o <title> da página.

**Para *"<title>"* e "*título principal*" diferentes:**  
preencher o <title> da página normalmente e colocar o "título principal" desejado no quadro abaixo (rosa).

# As Universidades brasileiras nos rankings mundiais

- 1 Théry, H. (2010). Classificações de universidades mundiais, "Xangai" e outras . Estudos Avançados, [(...)](https://journals.openedition.org/confins/58999#ftn1)

1Um artigo publicado na revista *Estudos avançados**[1](https://journals.openedition.org/confins/58999#ftn1)* tinha analisado *o Academic Ranking of World Universities (Arwu),* conhecido como “ranking de Xangai”, examinando mais de perto seu funcionamento e plotando seus dados em um mapa-múndi para mostrar a geografia do que ele considera “as principais universidades do mundo”. Como outros rankings foram elaborados em resposta às deficiências e vieses dele, três deles também tinham analisados e mapeados.

2A edição de 2024 do Arwu, publicada em 15 de agosto de 204, oferece uma ocasião para fazer um balanço da sua evolução, mais uma vez mapeando seus resultados e comparando-os com os de outros rankings, e depois situar as universidades brasileiras nesse contexto global.

3O primeiro mapa mostra as 100, 500 e 1.000 melhores universidades por país, de acordo com essa classificação. O segundo compara a posição das universidades brasileiras nos rankings Arwu 2024 e 2008 (que foi usado no artigo anterior) e em dois outros rankings para 2024, o do *Center for World University Ranking* (CWUR) e o do *Times Higher Education*. Como os resultados desse último são bastante diferentes daqueles do Arwu (devido aos critérios em que se baseia), um terceiro mapa traça uma tipologia que esclarece os resultados diferenciados das universidades brasileiras.

## [O contexto global](https://journals.openedition.org/confins/58999#tocfrom1n1)

4O ranking Arwu compara instituições de ensino superior. Em 2024 ele classificou 1.000 instituições, levando em conta seis indicadores, principalmente relacionados à pesquisa: o número de ganhadores do Prêmio Nobel e da Medalha Fields entre seus ex-alunos e professores, o número de citações de pesquisadores, o número de artigos publicados nas revistas *Science* e *Nature*, o número de artigos no *Science Citation Index* e no *Social Sciences Citation Index*.

5Em termos de número de universidades por milhão de habitantes, o “Ocidente” (América do Norte, Europa, Austrália) continua dominando, com os Estados Unidos na liderança entre as 100 e 500 melhores. Mas a China é agora o país com o maior número de universidades entre as 1.000 melhores da lista, e outros países asiáticos estão seguindo o seu exemplo: a Coreia do Sul sobe 7 posições e o Japão 2, quando se passa das 500 para as 1.000 melhores.

6Usando o mesmo cálculo, o sul da Europa sobe (Itália e Espanha ganham 15 posições) e o norte da Europa desce (Bélgica cai 2 posições, Holanda e Suécia 3, França 4). A queda no número de países menores entre os 1.000 primeiros é, sem dúvida, parcialmente devida a um efeito de tamanho: a Suíça cai 15 posições, a Dinamarca 17, Israel 18, enquanto o Brasil sobe 10 posições.

Figura 1 Ranking Arwu 2024, das 100, 5000 e 1000 melhores universidades por país

[![Figura 1 Ranking Arwu 2024, das 100, 5000 e 1000 melhores universidades por país](https://journals.openedition.org/confins/docannexe/image/58999/img-1-small480.jpg)](https://journals.openedition.org/confins/docannexe/image/58999/img-1-small580.jpg)

## [Situação das universidades brasileiras](https://journals.openedition.org/confins/58999#tocfrom1n2)

7Existem outros rankings além do Arwu, em 2010, dois tinham sido analisados: o da *École des Mines de Paris*, baseado no número de ex-alunos entre os diretores das 500 maiores empresas do mundo, e o do laboratório *Cybermetrics*, que analisava a qualidade da informação nos sites das universidades. Nenhum deles é mais produzido, e foi necessário procurar outros.

- Entre eles está o da *QS University ranking* publicado desde 2011 por Quacquarelli Symonds, após seu rompimento com o *The Times* (veja abaixo) e a classificação de Leiden. Nenhum deles foi satisfatório, o primeiro porque era muito redundante com o Arwu, o segundo porque baseado exclusivamente em indicadores bibliométricos). Dois outros foram escolhidos

-   - 2 Desde 2016, sua sede está localizada nos Emirados Árabes Unidos.

    O jornal britânico *The Times* tem publicado o *THE World University Rankings* desde 2004 em sua publicação mensal *Times Higher Education*. O *Center for World University Rankings (CWUR)*, criado em 2012 em Jeddah, na Arábia Saudita[2](https://journals.openedition.org/confins/58999#ftn2), avalia a qualidade da educação, empregabilidade, corpo docente e pesquisa. Em 2019, as suas classificações foram ampliadas, com 20.966 instituições classificadas e as melhores compondo sua lista Global 2000.

8A tabela das 10 melhores universidades brasileiras de acordo com os quatro rankings (Arwu 2008 e 2024, CWUR e THE) mostra que todas estão localizadas no Sudeste e no Sul: quatro no estado de São Paulo, duas no Rio de Janeiro e no Rio Grande do Sul, e uma em Minas Gerais e Santa Catarina. Apenas uma universidade, a Universidade de São Paulo - USP, está entre as 200 melhores do mundo.

Quadro 1 As dez primeiras universidades brasileiras nos quatro rankings

- Universidade THE 2024 CWUR 2024 Arwu2024 Arwu 2008
- Universidade de São Paulo -USP 201–250 103 101-150 101-151
- Universidade de Campinas - Unicamp 351–400 346 401-500 201-302
- Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Sul - UFRGS 601–800 461 401-500 402-503
- Universidade Estadual Paulista - Unesp 601–800 419 401-500 402-503
- Universidade Federal de Rio de Janeiro - UFRJ 601–800 361 501-600 303-401
- Universidade Federal de São Paulo - UNIFESP 801–1000 589 701-800
- Universidade Federal de Minas Gerais - UFMG 801–1000 500 501-600 303-401
- Universidade Federal de Santa Catarina - UFSC 801–1000 719 701-800
- Pontifícia Universidade Católica de Rio de Janeiro (PUC-Rio) 801–1000 1610
- Pontifícia Universidade Católica do Rio Grande do Sul (PUCRS) 1001–1200 1504

9A Figura 2 plota todas as universidades que aparecem em pelo menos um dos rankings e mostra que seu número aumentou entre o Arwu 2008 e o Arwu 2024, com a inclusão de mais universidades no Sudeste-Sud e algumas no Nordeste e no Norte. A lista de classificação da CWRU inclui mais universidades nessas regiões e THE ainda mais, com alguns casos (quadrados azuis) em que é a única a incluí-las: isso se explica pelo fato de levar em conta critérios que as outras classificações ignoram. Essa particularidade justifica que se preste mais atenção a esse ranking.

Figura 2 As universidades brasileiras em quatro rankings mundiais

[![Figura 2 As universidades brasileiras em quatro rankings mundiais](https://journals.openedition.org/confins/docannexe/image/58999/img-2-small480.jpg)](https://journals.openedition.org/confins/docannexe/image/58999/img-2-small580.jpg)

## [Critères et typologie du *THE World University Ranking*](https://journals.openedition.org/confins/58999#tocfrom1n3)

10O *THE World University Ranking* classifica as universidades em termos de suas missões essenciais: *Teaching* (ambiente de aprendizagem), *Research environment* (volume, orçamentos e reputação), *Research quality* (resultados da pesquisa), *Industry* (relações com empresas e transferência de conhecimento) e *International outlook* (abertura internacional em funcionários, alunos e pesquisa). Há também uma série de classificações regionais e temáticas: universidades árabes, asiáticas, latino-americanas, “reputação mundial” e universidades jovens. O *Impact Ranking*, criado em 2019, avalia as universidades em relação aos Objetivos de Desenvolvimento Sustentável (ODDs) das Nações Unidas.

11A Tabela 2 foi construída atribuindo-se uma pontuação de 100 para cada critério à mais bem classificada das dez, e uma pontuação proporcional à sua pontuação THE às demais. Para os quatro primeiros critérios, a USP ficou em primeiro lugar, para relações com empresas, a Universidade Federal do Rio de Janeiro - UFRJ e para abertura internacional, a Pontifícia Universidade Católica do Rio de Janeiro (PUC-Rio).

Quadro Pontuações das dez melhores universidades brasileiras no THE World University Ranking

| Universidade | *Overall* | *Teaching* | *Research environment* | *Research quality* | *Industry* | *International outlook* |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Universidade de São Paulo -USP | 100 | 100 | 100 | 100 | 84 | 98 |
| Universidade de Campinas - Unicamp | 88 | 84 | 75 | 94 | 81 | 94 |
| Universidade Estadual Paulista - Unesp | 66 | 69 | 55 | 66 | 50 | 89 |
| Universidade Federal de Rio de Janeiro - UFRJ | 66 | 70 | 59 | 64 | 100 | 83 |
| Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Sul - UFRGS | 66 | 61 | 37 | 94 | 65 | 79 |
| Pontifícia Universidade Católica de Rio de Janeiro (PUC-Rio) | 58 | 56 | 50 | 65 | 78 | 100 |
| Universidade Federal de Santa Catarina - UFSC | 58 | 54 | 36 | 73 | 79 | 82 |
| Universidade Federal de São Paulo - UNIFESP | 58 | 56 | 37 | 84 | 58 | 81 |
| Universidade Federal de Minas Gerais - UFMG | 58 | 67 | 38 | 76 | 63 | 77 |
| Pontifícia Universidade Católica do Rio Grande do Sul (PUCRS) | 51 | 55 | 28 | 74 | 48 | 81 |

12Analisando os critérios nos quais o *THE World University Rankings* se baseia, pode-se esboçar uma explicação da situação relativa das universidades brasileiras.

13A Figura 3, baseada em uma classificação hierárquica ascendente (CAH) que agrupa os objetos observados de acordo com seu desvio do perfil geral, divide as universidades presentes nas quatro classificações em cinco classes:

- - A primeira (em vermelho) agrupa as que estão bem acima da média (barras horizontais à direita) para os cinco critérios;

- - A segunda (em laranja) as que estão um pouco acima da média (barras horizontais à direita) para os cinco critérios;

- - A terceira (em verde) as que estão acima da média para o relacionamento com as empresas;

- - A quarta (em azul claro) aquelas que estão abaixo da média (barras horizontais à esquerda) para todos os cinco critérios;

- - A quinta (em azul escuro) aquelas que estão bem abaixo da média (barras horizontais à esquerda) para todos os cinco critérios.

Figura 3 Tipologia em função dos critérios do THE World University Rankings

[![Figura 3 Tipologia em função dos critérios do THE World University Rankings](https://journals.openedition.org/confins/docannexe/image/58999/img-3-small480.jpg)](https://journals.openedition.org/confins/docannexe/image/58999/img-3-small580.jpg)

# Lista de ministros da Agricultura e Pecuária do Brasil

Esta é uma **lista de [ministros da Agricultura e Pecuária](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministério_da_Agricultura_e_Pecuária "Ministério da Agricultura e Pecuária")** do [Brasil](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brasil "Brasil").[[1]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lista_de_ministros_da_Agricultura_e_Pecu%C3%A1ria_do_Brasil#cite_note-ministerio-1)

Até 1892, com a denominação de Secretaria de Estado dos Negócios da Agricultura, Comércio e Obras Públicas, tinha responsabilidades tanto sobre a [agricultura](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agricultura "Agricultura") quanto o [transporte](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transporte "Transporte"), por isso a [lista de Ministros dos Transportes do Brasil](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lista_de_ministros_dos_Transportes_do_Brasil "Lista de ministros dos Transportes do Brasil") repete o nome dos ministros da Agricultura até 1892.[[1]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lista_de_ministros_da_Agricultura_e_Pecu%C3%A1ria_do_Brasil#cite_note-ministerio-1)

> Abstract:The high compute cost associated with pretraining large language models limits their research. Two strategies have emerged to address this issue: domain specialization and pretraining with high-quality data. To explore these strategies, we specialized the Mistral-7B model with 1.9 billion unique tokens from reputable Brazilian legal sources and conducted few-shot evaluations on legal and general knowledge test suites. conversa_com_ferramentas.content:
# Juru: Legal Brazilian Large Language Model from Reputable Sources

Roseval Malaquias Junior Affiliation: Computer Science Department, University of São Paulo, São Carlos, São Paulo, Brazil  
, E-mail <roseval@usp.br> Affiliation: Maritaca AI, Campinas, São Paulo, Brazil E-mail [{ramon, rodrigo}@maritaca.ai](mailto:%7Bramon,%20rodrigo%7D@maritaca.ai) Ramon Pires Roseli A. F. Romero Affiliation: Computer Science Department, University of São Paulo, São Carlos, São Paulo, Brazil  
, E-mail <roseval@usp.br> Rodrigo Nogueira E-mail <rafrance@icmc.usp.br> Affiliation: Maritaca AI, Campinas, São Paulo, Brazil E-mail [{ramon, rodrigo}@maritaca.ai](mailto:%7Bramon,%20rodrigo%7D@maritaca.ai)

###### Abstract

The high compute cost associated with pretraining large language models limits their research. Two strategies have emerged to address this issue: domain specialization and pretraining with high-quality data. To explore these strategies, we specialized the Mistral-7B model with 1.9 billion unique tokens from reputable Brazilian legal sources and conducted few-shot evaluations on legal and general knowledge test suites. Our model, Juru, demonstrates the benefits of domain specialization by achieving improved performance on legal benchmarks, even with a reduced amount of pretraining data. However, this domain specialization through continued pretraining comes at the cost of increased forgetting in unrelated domains, as evidenced by performance degradation on general knowledge test suites in both Portuguese and English. This study contributes to the growing body of scientific evidence showing that pretraining data selection may enhance the performance of large language models, enabling the exploration of these models at a lower cost. Juru is publicly available at <https://huggingface.co/roseval/Juru-7B>.

###### Keywords:

Domain Specialization Continued Pretraining Legal Language Models Low-Resource Pretraining

## 1 Introduction

Large Language Models (LLMs) are commonly trained on vast amounts of general-purpose data sourced from internet snapshots, such as the CommonCrawl [[3](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.18140v2#bib.bib3 ""), [4](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.18140v2#bib.bib4 ""), [32](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.18140v2#bib.bib32 "")] and C4 [[32](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.18140v2#bib.bib32 ""), [34](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.18140v2#bib.bib34 "")]. Scaling laws [[14](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.18140v2#bib.bib14 "")] support this paradigm, suggesting more capable models with increased data and trainable parameters. As a result, LLMs developed through this method demonstrate the ability to address tasks across multiple languages and domains [[20](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.18140v2#bib.bib20 "")].

The significant computational resources required for pretraining with such massive datasets pose a challenge for research, limiting the exploration of their capabilities. However, it is possible to observe competitive results on a smaller scale through the application of continued pretraining.
In the literature, the selection of domain-specific data [[8](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.18140v2#bib.bib8 ""), [9](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.18140v2#bib.bib9 ""), [22](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.18140v2#bib.bib22 "")] from reputable sources [[12](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.18140v2#bib.bib12 ""), [18](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.18140v2#bib.bib18 ""), [21](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.18140v2#bib.bib21 "")] stands out.

The large general-purpose pretraining of LLMs promotes general factual knowledge and language comprehension. Therefore, continued pretraining on the same scale and scope might not be necessary to improve LLMs’ performance.
By employing domain-specific data from reputable sources, we postulate that an LLM initially trained on general-purpose data can improve its performance in a specific domain with minimal additional data, although this may come at the expense of performance degradation in other domains.

To test this hypothesis, we specialized the Mistral-7B [[15](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.18140v2#bib.bib15 "")] model for the Brazilian legal domain, using <!-- MathML: <math intent=":literal" display="inline" alttext="1.9" id="S1.p4.m1"><semantics><mn>1.9</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.9</annotation></semantics></math> --> 1.91.9 billion unique tokens sourced mainly from academic studies from reputable sources. The resulting model, Juru, was evaluated on multiple-choice test suites covering both Brazilian legal knowledge and general knowledge domains. Our objective is to assess the impact of incorporating exclusively domain-specific data during continued pretraining on the model’s performance.

Across the proposed pretraining, our model demonstrated enhanced performance on the legal test suite, while exhibiting a decrease in performance on the general knowledge test suites. In particular, a more pronounced decrease was observed on the English test suite compared to the Portuguese one, suggesting that previously acquired knowledge is better retained when it shares greater similarity with the target domain of specialization. These results contribute to the growing body of scientific evidence supporting the effectiveness of specialized pretraining for improving the performance of generalist models on specific domains. Such specialization may facilitate their research by reducing the compute cost associated with training. Additionally, the resulting model, Juru, is publicly released to support further research on domain specialization through continued pretraining. To the best of our knowledge, Juru is the first LLM pretrained for the Brazilian legal domain.

## 2 Related Work

The increasing scale of LLMs, in both parameter numbers and training data, has led to the emergence of previously unseen abilities in smaller-scale models [[33](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.18140v2#bib.bib33 "")]. Recent advances have enabled these models to achieve human-level performance across various tasks that require textual comprehension, specialized knowledge, mathematical reasoning, multilingualism, programming, and image interpretation [[20](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.18140v2#bib.bib20 "")]. With such results, it is arguable that these models demonstrate the capacity to integrate these diverse skills in a cohesive manner.

Language and domain specialization have become effective strategies for ensuring that LLMs bring tangible benefits in real-world applications. Recent works have shown that continued pretrained in language-specific corpora, particularly in Portuguese [[1](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.18140v2#bib.bib1 ""), [17](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.18140v2#bib.bib17 ""), [22](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.18140v2#bib.bib22 "")], enhances significantly the performance of downstream tasks without the need to increase the parameter count.

The Brazilian legal field emerges as a relevant example of such domain specialization, as previous studies have underscored the performance of language models pretrained on legal corpora [[9](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.18140v2#bib.bib9 ""), [24](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.18140v2#bib.bib24 "")].
However, those models are encoder-only, lacking the ability to generate text sequentially, which is essential for several legal applications.

SaulLM-7B [[8](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.18140v2#bib.bib8 "")] is the first LLM pretrained to tackle the nuances of legal languages and follow instructions to support conversation interactions. Starting from Mistral-7B [[15](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.18140v2#bib.bib15 "")], the model was pretrained on 30 billion tokens of an English legal dataset. In a subsequent study, Colombo et al. [[7](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.18140v2#bib.bib7 "")] scaled this approach to a Mixture-of-Experts architecture. The authors continually pretrained Mixtral-54B and Mixtral-141B on 540 billion tokens of English legal texts, producing SaulLM-54B and SaulLM-141B. While these larger models achieve higher performance on most in-domain tasks, their increased size correlates with lower performance on certain legal tasks.

To the best of our knowledge, Juru is the first LLM pretrained for the Brazilian legal domain. Our experiments show that, relative to its base model, Juru achieves superior performance on in-domain tasks. However, its performance deteriorates on tasks beyond the Brazilian legal domain.

## 3 Methodology

In this section, we describe the gathering and curation of data from public sources within the Brazilian legal domain, as well as the pretraining of the Juru model, including its base model, hyperparameters, and optimization methods.

### 3.1 Pretraining Data

We conducted web scraping of academic papers in Portuguese within the Brazilian legal domain, prioritizing data with educational value.

Academic papers were scraped from various reputable sources that catalog research from Brazilian higher education institutions and national journals. Each platform offers filters for extracting Brazilian papers exclusively in Portuguese, accessible for non-commercial distribution. Also, we scraped the LexML11 1 [https://www.lexml.gov.br](https://www.lexml.gov.br/ "") database, focusing on a subset of Brazilian federal laws.

A total of 13,278 documents were extracted from academic paper databases. Nearly <!-- MathML: <math display="inline" alttext="99\%" intent=":literal" id="S3.SS1.p3.m1"><semantics><mrow><mn>99</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">99\%</annotation></semantics></math> --> 99%99\% of these documents are in Portable Document Format (PDF). Hence, we used Marker22 2 <https://github.com/VikParuchuri/marker> for extracting text from these documents.

Texts from 14,743 federal laws were extracted from the LexML database. Additionally, the dataset from the study by Sakiyama et al. [[27](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.18140v2#bib.bib27 "")] was added to the pretraining dataset, consisting of 32,535 legal documents distributed between decisions and judgments from the Brazilian Supreme Federal Court.

After extracting the documents, they were automatically curated using the filter proposed by Rae et al. [[25](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.18140v2#bib.bib25 "")], adapted for Portuguese. This filter removes documents that are unlikely to be predominantly natural language, such as tables or long lists, as they could hinder the learning process of the LLM.

### 3.2 Juru Model

The Juru model extends the causal language modeling pretraining of a Mistral-7B model, without instruction finetuning. We employed the t5x and seqio frameworks [[26](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.18140v2#bib.bib26 "")] for the proposed pretraining.

Although more recent models [[10](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.18140v2#bib.bib10 ""), [11](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.18140v2#bib.bib11 "")] of comparable size have demonstrated superior performance compared to Mistral-7B, we chose Mistral-7B due to its earlier release date. This decision aims to reduce the risk of data contamination in our test suites.

For the pretraining hyperparameters, we employed the AdaFactor optimizer [[30](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.18140v2#bib.bib30 "")] without factorization, with a first-order momentum of <!-- MathML: <math display="inline" intent=":literal" alttext="0.9" id="S3.SS2.p3.m1"><semantics><mn>0.9</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.9</annotation></semantics></math> --> 0.90.9 and a second-order momentum of <!-- MathML: <math alttext="1-k^{-0.8}" intent=":literal" display="inline" id="S3.SS2.p3.m2"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>k</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>0.8</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1-k^{-0.8}</annotation></semantics></math> --> 1−k−0.81-k^{-0.8}, where <!-- MathML: <math intent=":literal" alttext="k" display="inline" id="S3.SS2.p3.m3"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> --> kk represents the current training step. Additionally, we applied dynamic weight decay by <!-- MathML: <math intent=":literal" alttext="lr^{2}" display="inline" id="S3.SS2.p3.m4"><semantics><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>r</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">lr^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> --> l​r2lr^{2}, with <!-- MathML: <math intent=":literal" display="inline" alttext="lr" id="S3.SS2.p3.m5"><semantics><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">lr</annotation></semantics></math> --> l​rlr as the current learning rate value, and global norm clipping of <!-- MathML: <math alttext="1.0" intent=":literal" display="inline" id="S3.SS2.p3.m6"><semantics><mn>1.0</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.0</annotation></semantics></math> --> 1.01.0.

## 4 Evaluation

Evaluating LLMs for text generation poses challenges due to the subjective nature of emerging skills such as natural language understanding and domain expertise, alongside their ability to integrate these skills for problem-solving. Given their broad capabilities, evaluating with open-ended questioning provides insights into the models’ knowledge representation and their capacity to generate human-like responses [[35](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.18140v2#bib.bib35 "")].

However, the evaluation of responses to open-ended questions poses inherent difficulties. Human evaluation is resource-intensive, requiring expertise in specific domain tasks and training in evaluation methodology for experimental robustness. Additionally, relying solely on SOTA LLMs for evaluation may yield a low correlation with human judges due to specific vocabulary and knowledge of a target domain. Hence, there’s an increasing emphasis on evaluating these models using standardized multiple-choice exams, such as those used in university admission processes [[2](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.18140v2#bib.bib2 ""), [5](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.18140v2#bib.bib5 ""), [19](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.18140v2#bib.bib19 ""), [23](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.18140v2#bib.bib23 ""), [28](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.18140v2#bib.bib28 "")]. Such exams cover diverse topics and skills, proving advantageous for LLM evaluation.

We investigate how continued pretraining through domain specialization influences both knowledge learning and forgetting. Hence, we evaluate the specialized Juru model on three standardized multiple-choice test suites: Brazilian legal knowledge, representing the target domain of our specialization; Portuguese general knowledge, which share the same language as the target domain but do not assess legal knowledge; and English general knowledge, whose distribution is closer to the original English-centric training data of Mistral-7B.

For all test suites, we adopt accuracy as the primary evaluation metric. We group all editions of the same exam administered within a given year into a single evaluation group. When aggregating multiple exams, we report the mean accuracy. Lastly, we employ few-shot learning with three examples during our evaluation, as the model was trained solely for text completion and did not undergo any instruction finetuning.

### 4.1 Brazilian Legal Knowledge

For evaluating the Juru model, we used questions from six Bar Association Exams (OAB) of <!-- MathML: <math display="inline" alttext="2024" intent=":literal" id="S4.SS1.p1.m1"><semantics><mn>2024</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2024</annotation></semantics></math> --> 20242024 and <!-- MathML: <math display="inline" alttext="2023" intent=":literal" id="S4.SS1.p1.m2"><semantics><mn>2023</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2023</annotation></semantics></math> --> 20232023, and two National Judiciary Exams (ENAM) of <!-- MathML: <math alttext="2024" display="inline" intent=":literal" id="S4.SS1.p1.m3"><semantics><mn>2024</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2024</annotation></semantics></math> --> 20242024. ### 4.2 Portuguese General Knowledge

Pires et al. [[22](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.18140v2#bib.bib22 "")] observed a performance degradation on English benchmarks following the specialization of an English-centric LLM for Portuguese. These results raise the following question: Is catastrophic forgetting limited to cross-linguistic domain specialization, or does specializing in a specific domain within a single language also lead to forgetting of general knowledge in that language?

To address this question, we examined the impact of specializing the Juru model in the Brazilian legal domain on its performance in Portuguese general knowledge tasks, using the multiple-choice exams listed in Table [3](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.18140v2#S4.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 4.2 Portuguese General Knowledge ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ Juru: Legal Brazilian Large Language Model from Reputable Sources"), comprising a total amount of 2,123 questions.

Table 3: Configuration of Portuguese general knowledge test suite.

Following Almeida et al. [[1](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.18140v2#bib.bib1 "")], we ignore all the questions that require image understanding. Some exams have captions describing the image contents. In those cases, we incorporate them into the exact position the images would appear.

### 4.3 English General Knowledge

Unlike the Sabiá [[22](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.18140v2#bib.bib22 "")] model, which underwent extensive continued pretraining, the Juru model was trained for fewer steps due to the smaller size of its legal specialization dataset. While Pires et al. [[22](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.18140v2#bib.bib22 "")] observed a loss of English knowledge in their model after extended training on Portuguese data, their experiments involved a significantly longer training regime and a more diverse dataset. This raises another question: Can shorter, domain-specific pretraining mitigate or prevent catastrophic forgetting of previously learned knowledge?

To investigate this, we evaluated the Juru model on the MMLU benchmark [[13](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.18140v2#bib.bib13 "")], a widely used test suite for assessing general knowledge and reasoning abilities in English [[15](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.18140v2#bib.bib15 ""), [20](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.18140v2#bib.bib20 ""), [31](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.18140v2#bib.bib31 "")]. While MMLU includes a broad range of subjects, such as STEM, humanities, law, and medicine, we restricted our evaluation to the college-level and high school-level subsets, amounting to 4,369 questions, as outlined in Table [4](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.18140v2#S4.T4 "Table 4 ‣ 4.3 English General Knowledge ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ Juru: Legal Brazilian Large Language Model from Reputable Sources").
